title: Young people in numbers
lede: Who young people in the UK are, where they are in life, what they deal with and what they hope for, in official figures first. Each chart says in plain words what it shows and what to be careful about, and where a figure covers only one nation it says so.
rule: Figures are copied from the source, never estimated here. Where the page works something out (a share from counts), it says so. Most social statistics are published nation by nation, so many figures here are for England only: the label says which.

kpis.t: people under 25 in England and Wales: 29.1% of everyone
of children in the UK live in relative poverty after housing costs
16 to 24 year olds not in education, employment or training: 13.0%
8 to 25 year olds had a probable mental disorder

figures.h: Who is under 25, by ethnic group
figures.says: About three in four under-25s are White and one in four are from an Asian, Black, Mixed or other ethnic group. Young people are more ethnically diverse than the population as a whole.
figures.care: Counts are worked out from the official age tables for each group, so they add up to 17,349,505 rather than the rounded 17.3 million. Census 2021 covers England and Wales only; Scotland and Northern Ireland ran their own censuses.

figures.h: Share of each ethnic group aged under 25
figures.says: Six in ten people from Mixed ethnic groups are under 25: the youngest group of all, with a median age of 19 against 43 for White groups. Decisions about young people affect minority ethnic communities more than their share of the population suggests.
figures.care: The White and Other percentages are summed from the published age bands rather than stated on the page.

figures.h: 5 to 15 year olds in Wales who can speak Welsh
figures.says: Young people are still the most likely of any age group to speak Welsh, but the share fell by six points in ten years and drove the fall in Welsh speakers overall. In January 2026, 21% of pupils in Wales were taught in Welsh-medium schools.
figures.care: The census asks a parent or the person themselves to rate their own ability, so it is a self-report, not a test.

figures.h: Languages at home
figures.says: Almost a quarter of five year olds in England are recorded as having English as an additional language: they speak another language at home.
figures.care: English as an additional language means exposure to another language at home, not low English ability.

figures.h: Probable mental disorder by age
figures.says: Around one in five at every stage, peaking at 17 to 19, the years of leaving school, exams and first jobs. From 17, rates among young women are twice those among young men.
figures.care: These are survey estimates from a questionnaire, not diagnoses, and the 2023 survey followed up the same young people first surveyed in 2017.

figures.h: Not in education, employment or training, by age

items.t: Not in education, employment or training (NEET)

figures.says: In England, 16 and 17 year olds must stay in education or training, so few are outside it. At 18 that rule ends and the rate more than triples: 18 is the cliff edge.
figures.care: Labour Force Survey estimates. Fewer people now answer the survey, which makes the figures less precise than they used to be.

figures.h: Out of work and learning, UK
figures.says: 13.0% of all 16 to 24 year olds, up 30,000 on a year before. 393,000 of them were looking for work; the rest were not, often because of ill health or caring.
figures.care: The next estimate is due on 26 November 2026, so this number will change soon.

figures.h: Children in relative poverty after housing costs
figures.says: About 27 in every 100 children live in a household with less than 60% of the middle income once rent or mortgage is paid. That is close to one in every classroom of four.
figures.care: DWP changed its method in March 2026 by linking benefit records, which broke the series. Compare this year with last year only, not with older headlines such as 4.45 million.

figures.h: Pupils with special educational needs
figures.says: One pupil in five in England has a special educational need, over 1.8 million in all. Plans have more than doubled since 2016.
figures.care: The rise partly reflects better identification and changes in how schools record needs, not only more need.

figures.h: Free school meals
figures.says: Over 2.2 million pupils are eligible for free school meals, up from 25.7% a year before.
figures.care: Eligibility depends on benefit rules, which change. A wider free school meals rule starts in September 2026, so next year's figure will jump for that reason alone.

figures.h: Children in care
figures.says: 67 in every 10,000 children are looked after by a council, slightly fewer than the year before.
figures.care: This counts children in care on one day. Many more spend some time in care during childhood.

figures.h: Child poverty after housing costs, by region and nation
figures.says: Child poverty is highest in the West Midlands, Yorkshire and London, and lowest in Scotland. London looks average before housing costs but among the worst after them: rent is the difference.
figures.care: Tiles are placed roughly where each area is; they are not to scale. These local-area figures use a different method from the 27% headline, so the UK reads 26.0% here.

figures.h: Make Your Mark 2024 turnout, by region and nation
figures.says: Whether young people get a vote depends on whether their council and schools run the ballot. Turnout was over 16% in the North East and North West but under 5% in London, the East Midlands and Wales.
figures.care: Scotland and Northern Ireland show 0.0% because the UK Youth Parliament ballot was barely run there (38 and 92 votes): they have their own youth parliament and assembly. The real 2024 turnouts there are not zero; they were counted elsewhere.

figures.h: What 16 and 17 year olds say they worry about
figures.says: Worries are close to home: jobs, exams and money top the list, each worrying three in four or more.
figures.care: A commissioned poll whose published summary does not give its sample size. The same release reports 69% worried about climate change from another question.

figures.h: Young carers who are themselves disabled
figures.says: About 120,000 children aged 5 to 17 in England (1.4%) and 8,200 in Wales give unpaid care. Young carers are three times as likely as other children to be disabled themselves.
figures.care: The census counts young carers that families report. Charities think many more are unreported.

figures.h: What young people say about politicians

items.t: Disagree that UK politicians listen to people their age
Agree that UK politicians listen to people their age
Feel they can influence decisions in their local area
Of those old enough, likely to vote at the next election

figures.says: Young people are active but do not feel heard: more than half say UK politicians do not listen to people their age, and fewer than one in three feel they can change things locally.
figures.care: A commissioned survey of 3,644 people. 'Likely to vote' is a stated intention, which usually runs ahead of what people actually do.

figures.h: Who is on the electoral register, by age
figures.says: Young people are far less likely to be registered than older people, so many cannot vote even when they are old enough. Registering early, from 14 in Scotland and Wales or 16 in England and Northern Ireland, closes the gap.
figures.care: These figures come from the Electoral Commission's 2023 study as reported by others; the Commission's own report was not read directly here. Attainers are people old enough to register but not yet old enough to vote.

figures.h: What they want most

items.t: Their top personal priorities are mental health, having enough money for the essentials and getting a good job they enjoy.
22% of 16 to 25 year olds say a stable job is one of their biggest goals in life.
Half of those out of work and learning say unemployment makes them feel hopeless about the future, and half do not feel in control of it, against 39% of their peers.

figures.says: The hopes are ordinary and practical: to be well, to get by and to do work that means something.
figures.care: Hopes come from surveys with different ages and questions, so they are shown in words rather than charted against each other.

figures.h: Absence from school, by free school meals eligibility
figures.says: Pupils from poorer homes miss twice as much school. Every missed day is also a missed club, trip, assembly or school council meeting.
figures.care: Absence has many causes, including illness and caring. The gap is a starting point, not an explanation.

figures.h: Who gets a voice, and who does not

items.t: Only 8.55% of 11 to 18 year olds voted in Make Your Mark 2024, and turnout ranged from over 70% in Westminster to under 5% in whole regions.
17 to 25 year olds with a probable mental disorder were three times as likely to be unable to afford activities such as sports, days out or socialising.

figures.says: Opportunity depends on where you live and what your family can afford. These gaps are why Amplify's inclusion and safeguarding screens matter.
figures.care: Area turnout depends on which schools took part, so a high or low figure says as much about the adults running the ballot as about young people.

against: Most figures are for England, because that is how they are published. Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland collect their own, often at different times and in different ways, so a UK picture has to be stitched together and can only be partly compared.
Survey figures describe the people who answered. Commissioned polls do not always publish their sample or methods, and are labelled Secondary here for that reason.
Numbers describe groups, never a person. A young person in a group with a high rate of anything is not more likely to be anything because of it.
